edges.description: The splice-acceptor substitution alters processing of the COX8A transcript.
The abnormal transcript is less abundant; the decay mechanism is not directly resolved.
The frameshift disrupts the sequence of the mature structural subunit.
Lower transcript availability compounds the abnormal coding sequence.
Loss of normal subunit function impairs holoenzyme stability, supported by wild-type complementation.
Reduced stable enzyme abundance accompanies reduced measured complex IV activity.
The biochemical lesion is associated with the reported neurological disease; the intervening neural mechanism has not been established.
White-matter injury accompanies the inherited enzyme defect; a specific ROS-mediated pathway is not demonstrated.
The reported mitochondrial disease includes lactic acidosis; the tissue-specific metabolic intermediates remain unresolved.

nodes.description: CRISPR/Cas9 targeting of exon 1 produced two viable clones with compound frameshift and in-frame mitochondrial-targeting-sequence lesions. Neither clone was a complete knockout. They reproduce reduced complex IV abundance and activity with variable retention of supercomplex-associated enzyme; they are not additional clinical genotypes. Transcriptome analysis did not detect induction of mtUPR/ISR genes in the assayed models.

nodes.description: The original patient line shows abnormal splicing, reduced stable complex IV and enzyme activity. Wild-type lentiviral COX8A restores enzyme stability and activity. Later work reuses this line and finds residual complex IV in supercomplexes with no mtUPR/ISR transcriptional induction. Daria Rotko's doctoral thesis also reports lower mitochondrial BK-alpha protein without a statistically significant KCNMA1 RNA decrease; its clinical significance is unresolved.
